data.name: Citizenship or Barbarism (= Ruralities) Notes by Óscar Gussinyer from the European Rural Parliament, Scotland
data.author: Oscar Gussinyer

metadata.metaTitle: Citizenship or Barbarism (= Ruralities) Notes by Óscar Gussinyer from the European Rural Parliament, Scotland
metadata.metaDescription: The article argues that ruralities are not remote but the living core of language, memory and ecological knowledge. In the face of a centralised system and a market that creates precarity, rural communities emerge as custodians of what still sustains life. The future, it suggests, depends on a polycentric regeneration grounded in self-determination, interdependence and the care of the commons.

children.text: <cite> Notes by Oscar Gussinyer from the European Rural Parliament, Scotland</cite>

In Scotland, during the European Rural Parliament, Theona Morrison of Scottish Rural Action —someone who lives and works on Uist, one of the few islands where Gaelic is still spoken— insisted that ruralities are not remote.

Suddenly, my mind began drifting through the meaning of that word. Remote is a relative adjective: it presupposes a centre. And that centre —whether a capital, a metropolis, or the global market— is always far from most ruralities.

It’s curious: Rome is farther from Barcelona than Beget, and yet no one in Barcelona would say Rome is remote. Remoteness, then, is not a matter of distance but of hierarchy; a moral geography of power that arranges the world into layers of centrality: from New York to Paris, from Madrid to Barcelona, down to county capitals that often believe themselves to be cities while someone, only a few kilometres away, already regards them as periphery.

I tried a mental exercise: what if we placed ruralities at the centre and cities on the margins? It struck me that, in truth, it is cities that have become remote from nature and its rhythms. It is an internal remoteness: a disconnection from the matrix that sustains life.

The Fluvià is much more than a line of water: it is a living organism that connects mountain and sea, volcanoes and wetlands, memory and future. But for decades we have treated it as a boundary, not as a bond.

Theona expressed it simply: we are the ones who keep alive the origins of our societies. The languages that gave us names, such as Gaelic or Catalan; the accumulated knowledge of plants, animals, climate, the cycles of ecosystems. We are the living memory of what still sustains life. And for a moment I understood that perhaps the future depends on this: on continuing to act as custodians of a knowledge that is not learned but inhabited.

While Theona continued speaking about the value ruralities hold precisely because we are far from central power, I remembered seeing the phrase rurality or barbarism. It made me reflect. Are they not, in fact, the same? Barbarism has often been the name the empire gives to what it cannot domesticate. Perhaps what ruralities across the planet share is being the least domesticated part of our society, the part that remembers that life is not administered but cultivated.
Because regenerating does not only mean restoring nature, but repairing the relationship. And that begins with a simple act: looking again.
Place-consciousness keeps us rooted while cities dissolve into abstraction and volatility. Who defines what is “civic”, and by what criteria? Is that not also a process of normalization?

Global markets steal our housing, youth exile intensifies, and industries that precarize us are imposed from above —economic realities that increasingly resemble techno-feudalism. Central governments take our resources and manage them without listening to lived experience; they disregard the fact that we are the old guard who protect culture and language.

After several workshops and sessions, I kept pondering: why have over a hundred people from organisations across Europe travelled all the way here? What is the true purpose of this gathering? I believe it is a movement of self-recognition. If the system still works, it is not because of its ability to manufacture products no one needs, nor because of its bureaucratic flair for complicating simple processes, but because of the resilience accumulated across millennia of co-evolution between communities and the ecosystems to which we belong.

When government institutionalises conservation, it severs a legacy of memory and narrative, and disempowers the community. When territory is planned from the capital, urban paradigms are imposed onto a rural reality that cannot be translated into metrics of performance or control. It is a daily micro-colonisation. Perhaps we are here because of this: because we refuse to relive processes of feudalism or colonisation. We come to ask legitimate questions: why does the government regulate us instead of regulating the market? Are we certain that civicism is the solution, and not dialogue? Or have we forgotten that coexistence is not achieved through rules but through relationship?

When I walk through our towns and mountains, I often ask myself why it isn’t the town councils themselves that break open the doors of empty buildings so new generations —of any background— can move in.

Why do we put a price on our legacy? How is it that the homes that once safeguarded the territory and upheld food sovereignty have become, all across Europe, currency —commodities where millionaires invest their privilege?

How can we allow global industries to internalise our territorial stewardship as profit while externalising poverty, nitrates, and CO₂ as if they were inevitable residues of progress? When land is treated as an asset, everything alive becomes an accounting variable. Why is Corporate Social Responsibility optional —and mostly a tool for greenwashing? How is it that we still haven’t dared to question private property, that invisible pillar that turns care into dominion? When did we stop understanding that inheritance is not individual but collective, that the territory does not belong to us but entrusts us with its continuity?

Is it not obvious that territorial precariousness affects the whole community, no matter how many walls we build? The people who arrive on foot or by boat are, in the end, margins like us, pushed by the same system that empties our towns and concentrates wealth in the centres. The challenges of overpopulation and mass migration, in a world undergoing climate crisis, are real —and they will not disappear by closing doors. Solidarity is not a moral choice: it is a natural law of life in common. What sense does it make to try to “fix Catalonia” while ignoring the fate of the planet, as if we could breathe a different air or eat from a different soil? No community can save itself alone in a world that is suffocating. Ruralities know this well: interdependence is not theory; it is daily experience.

We want to rise to the height of this historical moment: to welcome, reconcile, and sustain life without losing the sense of who we are —because that sense is what allows us to do it well. Therefore, this responsibility cannot justify the loss of our language or culture. Neither has ever been static: they have grown as nature grows, through interaction and metamorphosis, weaving new relationships without betraying their root. And yet, between those who want to close borders and those who treat culture as a folkloric residue, we have forgotten that life evolves neither through purity nor indifference, but through change, diversity, and mixture.

What we need is not more central control nor more institutional rigidity, nor the fear of those who confuse love of the land with retreat. What we need is self-determination, capacities, resilience, and flexibility to regenerate from within.

Only thus can we show that our language and culture are not borders that separate, but living sources that connect, that offer meaning in a disoriented world, and that can remind everyone —including cities— that caring for what is ours is the only sincere way to care for what is common.

This is why we feel an immediate affinity with other ruralities around the planet. When a community learns to sustain itself through its singularities, it recognises the same sensitivity in others. We share a common thread of dependence on land and life, a way of inhabiting the world that still knows how to recognise limit and reciprocity. We have more in common with someone planting rice in Mali or herding sheep in Iceland than with someone managing a city as if it were an algorithm. And this is not a slight: it is a simple affirmation of shared belonging. In our generation we are cultivating a new way of thinking —urban and global, yes— but can that way of thinking survive on its own?

I do not doubt that technology and urbanities contribute value; what I wonder is whether, deep down, they have come to believe they can leave us behind, as if ruralities were merely a previous stage of their own history. Perhaps ruralities are not obsolete: perhaps it is urbanities that have forgotten where they come from and what sustains them. Perhaps they are not the next evolutionary level, but the reflection of a mindset closed in on itself —a mindset that does not ask because it believes it already knows, that does not listen because it fears silence, and that does not self-critique because it confuses progress with perfection.

We are now told that the main problem is the rise of the far right, and that it emerges from ruralities. Should this frighten us —or should the political party system itself, which has been nurturing it for decades, frighten us more? Perhaps the question is not who occupies power, but what kind of thinking sustains it.

Are frustration, anger, and helplessness not what drive so many people in our territories toward reactionary proposals? Maybe the far right is not an anomaly but the visible decomposition of a system that no longer knows how to regenerate —a political body exhausted yet still moving by inertia, like an organism that mistakes motion for life.

When a system stagnates, what emerges is not its opposite but its shadow. And that shadow takes the form of authoritarian power promising order where there is only disorder. But the problem is not the monster: it is the ecosystem that makes it possible.

Two patterns sustain this decay: the centralist structure, which perpetuates inequality and privilege, and the incompetence of those who lead, incapable of serving. Both feed each other: a system that concentrates power can only produce fragile leadership; and fragile leadership can only survive by maintaining concentrated power. It is a closed, self-referential loop that expels diversity and punishes initiative.
Perhaps the greatest challenge is that the solution lies in the hands of the problem.

For the sixth time, over a hundred organisations and public administrations —from Greece to Iceland— have gathered to recognise ourselves as the voices of the margins. And in that recognition, the margins evolve into a polycentric, living, plural territorial distribution built not from domination but from complementary relationships.
